name: Emperor Wu of Han
info: Liu Che, seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, ruled China from 141 to 87 BCE, a reign of 54 years in which the empire expanded to Central Asia, Korea and Vietnam and Confucianism became the state doctrine.

facts.born: 156 BCE, on the day his father Liu Qi acceded as Emperor Jing of Han; son of Emperor Jing and Wang Zhi, of the Liu family of the Han dynasty
facts.died: 29 March 87 BCE, after a serious illness that began by 88 BCE; buried in the Maoling mound
facts.role: Prince of Jiaodong from 153 BCE; crown prince from 149 BCE; seventh emperor of the Han dynasty from 141 BCE until his death in 87 BCE
facts.known: the longest reign of an ethnic Han emperor; wars against the Xiongnu; the missions of Zhang Qian to the Western Regions; the annexation of Nanyue, Dian and Gojoseon; the promotion of Confucianism and the Imperial University; the Taichu calendar; the Imperial Music Bureau; harsh punishments and the witchcraft persecutions

t: Liu Che came to the throne at 15 in 141 BCE and, after the death of his grandmother Empress Dowager Dou in 135 BCE, ruled with full control of the government for the rest of a 54-year reign.

His armies drove the Xiongnu out of the Ordos Desert and Qilian Mountains, opened the way to Central Asia and annexed Nanyue, Dian and Gojoseon, while the cost of the wars brought new levies, famine and peasant revolts.

He promoted Confucian learning and strengthened the emperor's power over the prime minister, yet governed by harsh officials, and the witchcraft persecutions of his last years killed his own crown prince and many others.
dyk: Wu is said to have raised the Imperial Music Bureau to a prestigious institution; it collected folk songs from across the country and songs based on Central Asian tunes, and gave its name to the yuefu style of poetry.
ev: Liu Che is born on the day his father accedes as Emperor Jing
He succeeds to the throne at 15, and soon launches the Jianyuan Reforms, which his grandmother Empress Dowager Dou defeats
He sends Zhang Qian to seek the Yuezhi, the start of Han exploration of the Western Regions
At the Battle of Mobei the Han generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing force the Xiongnu chanyu north of the Gobi Desert
Han forces take Panyu and annex the whole of Nanyue, establishing ten commanderies
Han takes over the lands of Gojoseon and establishes four commanderies
Crown Prince Ju's revolt is crushed in Chang'an after five days of fighting; he and his mother Empress Wei die
Wu dies and the youngest son Liu Fuling succeeds as Emperor Zhao

sections.early:
Liu Che was the 11th son of Liu Qi, the oldest living son of Emperor Wen of Han. His mother Wang Zhi had earlier been married to a commoner, Jin Wangsun, and had a daughter by him. Her mother Zang Er was told by a soothsayer that both of her daughters would one day be greatly honoured, and offered them to the crown prince Liu Qi, forcibly divorcing Wang Zhi from her husband. Liu Qi became Emperor Jing of Han on the death of Emperor Wen in 156 BCE, and on that day Wang Zhi gave birth to Liu Che. She claimed to have dreamed during her pregnancy that a sun fell into her womb. Liu Che was made Prince of Jiaodong on 16 May 153 BCE and was said to be his father's favourite son from a very young age.

The empress, Empress Bo, had no children, and Liu Rong, the son of Lady Li, was made crown prince in 153 BCE. Emperor Jing's sister Princess Guantao, whose offer to marry her daughter to Liu Rong Lady Li had rudely rejected, instead proposed the marriage of her daughter Chen Jiao to the five-year-old Liu Che. Consort Wang accepted. Princess Guantao then criticised Lady Li before the emperor, and in 150 BCE Emperor Jing deposed Liu Rong, who was arrested two years later and killed himself in custody. Wang was made empress, and Liu Che became crown prince in 149 BCE. In 141 BCE Emperor Jing died and Liu Che ascended the throne as Emperor Wu at the age of 15.
sections.rise:
The Han court had until then followed a policy of non-interference, and kept the peace with the Xiongnu by periodic marriage alliances (heqin). It had also left the vassal states powerful enough to rebel in the Rebellion of the Seven States under Emperor Jing. In late 141 BCE Wu took the advice of Confucian scholars and launched the Jianyuan Reforms: endorsing Confucianism, sending noblemen back to their fiefs, removing unsanctioned checkpoints, prosecuting criminal nobles and recruiting talented commoners. His grandmother, Grand Empress Dowager Dou, who held real power and supported the conservatives, defeated the reforms. His supporters Dou Ying and Tian Fen lost their positions, and his two mentors Wang Zang and Zhao Wan were arrested and forced to commit suicide in prison. Wu then spent some years playing the part of a docile pleasure-seeker, while political enemies used the childlessness of Empress Chen Jiao to argue for replacing him with his cousin Liu An, King of Huainan.

Wu secretly recruited young supporters of ordinary background into middle-level posts, forming an "insider court" that reported directly to him and counterbalanced the "outsider court" of ministers. In 138 BCE he used an imperial decree to send a fleet to the aid of Dong'ou against Minyue without the tiger tally that his grandmother held. In the same year the concubine Wei Zifu became pregnant with his first child. Grand Empress Dowager Dou died in 135 BCE, leaving him in full control.
sections.deeds:
After 135 BCE Wu turned to expansion. The Battle of Mayi in 133 BCE, a failed plan to ambush a Xiongnu force of 30,000 with 300,000 Han soldiers, ended the policy of peace, and he changed the army from chariot and infantry to mobile cavalry. Between 127 and 119 BCE Wei Qing and his nephew Huo Qubing drove the Xiongnu from the Ordos Desert and Qilian Mountains, opening the Northern Silk Road, and 700,000 soldier-settlers were sent to colonise the Hexi Corridor. In 139 BCE he had sent Zhang Qian to the Yuezhi; Zhang returned in 126 BCE and regular embassies to the Western Regions followed. Han took Nanyue in 111 BCE, Dian in 109 BCE and Gojoseon in 108 BCE. In 102 BCE Li Guangli's second army forced Dayuan to surrender 3,000 of its horses after a first army had been defeated in 103 BCE.

At home he founded the Imperial University in 136 BCE and, in 106 BCE, divided the empire into 13 prefectures with a supervisor for each. The Taichu calendar of 104 BCE began the year with the first month. To pay for his spending, his agricultural minister Sang Hongyang devised state monopolies on salt and iron. He also introduced the practice of changing reign names, and worshipped the god Tai Yi and held the Feng and Shan sacrifices at Mount Tai.
sections.opponents:
Wu trusted officials who were harsh in punishment. One of them, Yi Zong, executed 200 prisoners who had committed no capital crime, and then their visiting friends. In 122 BCE Liu An and his brother Liu Ci were accused of plotting treason and killed themselves, and their families and many alleged conspirators were executed. In 117 BCE the minister Yan Yi, who had opposed a plan to extort double tribute from princes and marquesses, was executed for "internal defamation". When Li Ling surrendered to the Xiongnu in 99 BCE, Wu had his clan executed. Wu is said to have borne a grudge against the historian Sima Qian, whose Shiji was less flattering to him than he wished, and to have had him castrated.

The wars strained the people. After Mobei the Han lost almost 80% of their warhorses, new levies burdened the peasants, and a census showed a drop in population from famine and flight from taxes. About 100 BCE there were many peasant revolts, and an edict making officials answerable with their lives for unsuppressed revolts led them to hide the revolts. Wu's tours and search for immortality strained the treasury; twice a governor killed himself after failing to supply his whole train. The historian Michael Loewe called the reign the high point of "Modernist" policies. Wu is often compared to Qin Shi Huang, and historians have treated him with ambivalence. He incarcerated nearly two hundred thousand people in special prisons; of his twelve prime ministers, three were executed and two killed themselves in office.
sections.last:
In 96 BCE a series of witchcraft persecutions began. Wu, disturbed by a nightmare of being whipped by tiny puppets and by a sighting of an assassin who left no trace, ordered extensive investigations. Many accused, often high officials, were executed with their clans, beginning with the prime minister Gongsun He. The persecutions became tangled in a struggle over the succession. Crown Prince Ju disagreed with his father over policy, favouring leniency, and the official Jiang Chong and the eunuch Su Wen, who had accused him before, claimed to find witchcraft items in his palace; Ju knew he had been framed. In 91 BCE Ju killed Jiang. Wu, told falsely that Ju was staging a coup, ordered Prime Minister Liu Qumao to put it down. After five days of fighting in Chang'an, Ju fled and hanged himself when surrounded, and his mother Empress Wei Zifu killed herself.

Wu later came to see that many witchcraft accusations were false, had Su Wen burned and issued a public apology, the Repenting Edict of Luntai; wars and expansion generally ceased. By 88 BCE he was seriously ill. He chose his youngest son Liu Fuling, then six, as heir, named Huo Guang regent and ordered the execution of the boy's mother, Consort Zhao, for fear that she would become an uncontrollable empress dowager. He died in 87 BCE. Fuling succeeded as Emperor Zhao and Wu was buried at Maoling.
sections.legacy:
Wu roughly doubled the size of the Han empire, and much of the territory he annexed is now part of modern China. At its height its borders ran from the Fergana Valley in the west to northern Korea in the east and northern Vietnam in the south. Under him the Han dynasty opened trade with Central Asia, and contacts with western Eurasia greatly increased. Historians have treated him with ambivalence: he officially promoted Confucianism, yet like Qin Shi Huang personally governed by a Legalist system of rewards and punishments. He is said to have been extravagant and superstitious, and to have killed thousands of people and their families in the Liu An affair, the Hengshan case, the witchcraft prosecutions and Prince Ju's revolt.

His reforms strengthened the emperor's power at the expense of the prime minister, and the post of Shangshu, once a keeper of documents, became the emperor's close adviser, which it remained until the end of the imperial era. An examination of over 100 young scholars in 140 BCE, in which Dong Zhongshu argued for Confucianism, marks the start of its establishment as imperial doctrine, though it is unclear how far Wu himself decided this, since the prime minister Wei Wan was also a Confucian. His Imperial Music Bureau gave its name to the yuefu style of poetry, and the fu style took shape at his court around Sima Xiangru. Maoling was later looted by the Chimei.

summary: Emperor Wu of Han (156-87 BCE) ruled China for 54 years from 141 BCE. He drove back the Xiongnu, annexed lands from Central Asia to Korea and Vietnam and promoted Confucian learning, but his wars, taxes and witchcraft persecutions brought heavy suffering, including the death of his own crown prince.
notes: The article's Era names list the first reign name Jianyuan as 140 BC, while the text says the Jianyuan Reforms began in late 141 BC and that he acceded in 141 BC; 141 used.

Prince Ju's revolt is given as 91 BC in the Gongsun family passage (executions 'in 91 BC'); the article also dates Tian Qianqiu's report to 92 BC, before the revolt, which is inconsistent. The 'Repenting Edict' sequence is likewise confused. The text avoids dating Tian's report and the edict.
Wei Qing's death is given as 106 BC in one passage; left out. Death of Gongsun He is dated by implication to 91 BC or 96 BC (article inconsistent); only 'beginning with' is used.

Conquest of Nanyue: the article gives 135 BC for the Minyue attack on Nanyue in two places and mentions a 'Han-Nanyue War' return in 111 BC before the conquest section; the Minyue passages are muddled (king names Ying/Luo Ying, Yushan/Yushan) and are left out; Nanyue's annexation in 111 BC and ten commanderies kept.
The Gojoseon passage says 'Emperor Wei' and 'Jin's ambassadors'; left out. Wu's 'second invasion' of Korea and Canghai commandery 126 BC not used.
Sima Qian castration is stated flatly by the article without source or date; attributed here as the article states it, not given a year.
Mobei: the article says the Han lost almost 80% of their warhorses; used as given. 'Famines' stated in the article as the cause of the census drop; used.
The folk legend of 200 women executed at Maoling left out as legend; Huo Guang's 500 women omitted.
Date of Dayuan war: the text says the second army forced surrender of 3,000 'prized horses'; used.
Liu An suicide 122 BC given; article also says Liu An opposed the Minyue expedition in 135 BC.
Death date: the lede gives 29 March 87 BC; the body gives only 87 BC.
Born-fact: lifespan hedges not stated in the article; 'a serious illness that began by 88 BCE' paraphrases 'By 88 BC ... seriously ill'.
